Speed between questions comes first, so no loading spinners inside a lesson. No hearts, gems, combos or celebrations. No definitions or conjugations from the model’s memory. The data keeps its shape: columns can be added, not renamed.
The orchestrator. Dan routes the work, tests it and approves it. Nothing goes public, costs money, creates an account or deletes data without Dan.

Pull the latest version and test before every push, and never force a push. Testing is standard: a fast tier before the push, the full suite on GitHub after it.

Four scripts check the courses: the word audit, the every-lesson check, a screen-by-screen check, and one that merges their results. Counts go in the reply, with no spreadsheet unless Dan asks.

Required before every push. It taps through a real lesson on a simulated iPhone and iPad, and fails on an error, a dead tap, a frozen page, a late sound or too many audio players. Desktop passing says nothing about iPhone or iPad.
All work goes to one branch and one live site. A two-site setup is parked until testers arrive.
Each deploy takes the next animal in alphabetical order, Aardvark to Zebra, then round again. The push is refused if the number hasn’t moved on.

Never one audio player per recording, because that froze iPhones and iPads. At most twelve are kept and reused, and sounds for the current question and the next two are made ready ahead of time. Real iPhone behavior can be confirmed only on the devices.

Content moves from the workbook to the app in three steps: import it, check it against Tatoeba, Wiktionary and Lingua Libre, then build it into the app. The build fails if the checks disagree with the workbook.
Oaths, slurs, violence, stray English and official jargon never count toward a course’s A1 word list. What gets dropped is logged.
A hint that only says “present of kunne” is replaced with the real meaning, taken from that word’s own Wiktionary entry.
English shown to learners uses US spelling. The course language is never respelled, and a UK or US spelling is accepted in answers.
Scripts propose better sentences and answers; they are reviewed before any of them go into the next workbook.
Dan’s decisions and the native speaker’s corrections are kept in files the build reads. A corrected sentence is held back until the workbook has the fix.
A unit goes live only with Dan’s recorded approval. Sentences written for Tamago need a native-speaker check before testers.
Punctuation and extra spaces never count. In the default setting, a missing accent or capital is right but pointed out, and up to two typos are forgiven. Strict mode allows none.
A typo or accent that turns a word into another word the course teaches is wrong, never a typo.
A fresh session that didn’t build Tamago grades how it looks and feels. It doesn’t judge the French or the learning logic.

Use the live site as a new learner would, screenshot every screen, time the lesson, grade each criterion from 1 to 5 with evidence, and list the fixes in order. Change no code. When in doubt, give the lower grade.

Choose speed, less on screen and no game rewards. If two rules conflict, follow the newer one and log it.

The gather-only plan was replaced with a full run to the end of A1: gather, filter the word list, wire in privately, audit, add a mock exam, then review. Going live still waits for Dan. Greek, Czech, Hungarian and Finnish were dropped, and Norwegian was held.

Eight principles: recall beats rereading, forgetting is part of the design, adults can use a rule, language is sound first, help fades, practice looks like use, adults run their own learning, and what counts is what lasts.
Measured against Paul Nation’s four strands when this was written: deliberate study was strong, understanding and producing messages were weak, and fluency was missing.

Seven methods: about four new words at most, older material mixed in, wrong choices that test the grammar point, sound with every sentence, some speaking aloud, speaking from memory, and a short explanation of the mistake.

Nine methods: rounds spread over days, three correct answers on three different days, short passages, true statements, real questions, untimed fluency practice, hearing drills, short grammar notes, and whole phrases first.
“I can” statements are ticked only after a task. Ask for a when-and-where plan, never shame a missed day, and give real choice of topic.
Measure whether learners still recall an item a day or more later, how hard each round is, how long lessons take, and where hints are used.
Learning styles, input alone, machine-graded pronunciation, speed pressure, long explanations and rewards.
Small changes now, the bigger methods in later phases.

The research gives direction, not exact numbers. The limits are starting points to tune. The sources were checked to exist and their claims checked through abstracts, but the full papers weren’t read.
A question combines an item, a question type, a variant and a direction. One sentence can feed many questions.
From matching pairs to speaking from memory. Each trains one main skill. Speaking is never graded.
Each type can be asked in different ways. Variants are live, testing or off, and none are deleted.
The same content with less help each time: Exposure, Guided, Build, Partial Recall, Recall.
Take the items for the round, add no more than four new words, bring back one missed item, and make a wrong choice test the unit’s contrast.
